newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia bows to rebel demands on troops.
newsitem.headline: Colombia bows to rebel demands on troops.

text.p: President Ernesto Samper acceeded on Wednesday to demands from leftist guerrillas who took 60 soldiers prisoner three months ago, by ordering the demilitarization of huge swathes of Colombia's southern jungle in order to speed up the release of the soldiers.

Samper said that more than 5,400 square miles (14,000 sq km) of Caqueta province would be demilitarized between Dec. 6 and Dec. 16 -- mirroring almost exactly the terms set by the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) for the soldiers' safe release.
Military commanders previously said the FARC's conditions, outlined in a Sept. 30 communique, were impossible to meet.

"The government is willing to make a contribution to break the deadlock. This space and time frame is sufficient for the imprisoned troops to be moved and freed without the slightest risk to them or their captors," Samper said.
The troops were captured on Aug. 30 when the FARC overran a military outpost in Las Delicias in southern Putumayo province. At least 27 soldiers died in the attack.

Until now, the military said it would only clear a much smaller zone and for less than a week, warning that broader concessions would allow the FARC, which it accuses of drug trafficking, to ship precursor chemicals for cocaine manufacture into the area.

Underlying those concerns, which Samper appears to have overridden, were senior commanders' fears that the FARC would use the handover to score political points -- adding to the already humiliating military blow suffered by the army in the original attack.

"This seems a very positive move to us. The government's proposal is very close to what the FARC proposed two months ago. There are still some differences but these appear to be much less than before," Pierre Gassmann, head of the International Committee of the Red Cross in Colombia, told Reuters. He said the FARC had not yet sent any response.

The mothers' of the captured soldiers had become increasingly impatient at the deadlock between the government and the FARC, and earlier this month went on a week-long river trip in Caqueta province in a fruitless attempt to make direct contact with the rebels.
